playbook:
**Playbook — ref_estate**

- Net worth = cash + purchase price of deeds held, so buying at par costs me nothing in net worth. When an unowned tile is put to me and I can afford it, I buy, unless holding cash for a better tile shortly ahead clearly matters more.
- Rent paid out is a pure loss; rent collected is income. Prioritize buying high-rent tiles (best rent-to-price ratio first), especially ones opponents will land on often.
- Never let my balance drift so low that I must pass on a purchase. Buying early is fine, but I should keep a cash floor roughly equal to the price of the most valuable unowned tile on the circuit, minus expected salary, so I don't get priced out of a big buy late.
- When I land on an owned tile, I pay the rent immediately, add any incoming transfers since my last turn, and declare the correct new balance. Always reconcile with the bank's transfer log shown to me.
- When I pass or land on START, I collect the salary — this is easy to overlook; it's the main reliable income, so I always add it before deciding anything else that turn.
- Don't hoard cash for its own sake: an unspent 110 that never bought anything earned nothing. Idle cash only wins if opponents are even poorer; usually converting cash into deeds (which count at full price) is the stronger play.
- Track which opponents own which tiles from the transfer log so I can anticipate rent exposure on upcoming laps.
- Keep replies minimal: pay/buy/balance tokens with a sentence of reasoning at most. The decision, not the explanation, scores.

1.text:
Playbook for next time:

- Winning is declared cash plus purchase price of deeds held. A purchase converts cash 1:1 into net worth, so buying costs me nothing in score terms and gains me rent income. When an unowned property is offered and I can afford it, I buy it — always.
- Buy early, buy often. Every lap I hold no property is a lap I pay rent to others and collect none. The early game is when most properties are still unowned; my priority is to spend nearly all cash on deeds in the first half of the game.
- Do not hoard a large cash reserve "for safety." There is no downside risk to being cash-poor: rent obligations come out of the score either way, and unspent cash earns nothing. Only keep enough buffer to cover likely rents (roughly the highest single rent on the board, or a bit more).
- Exception: if buying would leave me unable to pay an imminent rent, and bankruptcy/penalty rules exist, check them first. If rent can simply be deducted, buy down to near-zero safely.
- When I must decline a purchase because cash is short, note it as a loss caused by over-renting or under-buying earlier — the fix is buying earlier, not conserving cash.
- Salary timing: passing START is worth 25, so my true affordable budget mid-game is last declared balance plus 25 if I'll pass START before the next purchase opportunity.
- Prefer high rent-to-price properties when choosing (rent/price ratios vary — e.g., rent ~20-25% of price is strong), but in practice the choice is usually "this property now or nothing," and the answer is now.
- Rent paid to others is a pure loss with no offsetting benefit. There is no way to avoid landing on owned tiles, so the only defense is owning tiles myself and ending the game with maximum deed value.
- At final scoring, if any purchase opportunity remains on the last lap, still buy: it's score-neutral at worst and adds rent if other players move after me.

What did not work: staying liquid and passing on purchases to keep a "healthy reserve" — I skipped a 120 property because I held only 100, and finished with cash I never needed. Spend the cash on deeds.

2.text:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

- Buy any unowned property I land on whenever my balance after purchase stays comfortably above zero — cash in hand earns nothing, but deeds count toward the final score at full purchase price and collect rent. Buying is nearly always score-neutral or better in the short run and profitable over laps.
- Exception: don't spend down to near-zero if a cheap high-rent tile is still unowned ahead of me (Depot, Mill). Keep roughly 50–60 in reserve mid-game so I can pounce on late opportunities.
- When a purchase would put me below zero or exactly at zero with rent still possible before my next salary, decline.
- Compute my balance from the ledger each turn, not just my last declaration: add salary when I pass START, add all "received since last turn" amounts, subtract any rent I pay this turn. Declare that exact number — accurate books matter since the score is my declared cash plus deed value.
- Prioritize high rent-to-price tiles when choosing between purchases if I ever face a constrained budget: Wharf and Exchange are the best deals per the numbers shown; Terrace and Depot are mediocre but still worth owning if affordable.
- Never decline a buy just because I'd be left "thin" in the early laps — rent flows in faster than expected once others own tiles, and being too conservative on mid-priced tiles (like Mill at 90 with 80 in hand was borderline) cost me income. If the shortfall is only 10–20, sometimes waiting one lap for rent/salary to arrive is the right call — check whether I'm likely to pass START before landing on the tile again.
- Track which tiles remain unowned: once most are owned, I should hoard cash instead of waiting for buys, since unspent cash counts 1:1 toward the final score anyway. A declined buy isn't lost value — it's just deferred.
- When rent is due, pay it promptly and factor it into the declared balance in the same turn.
- Endgame (last lap): if I pass START, always collect the salary. Convert any final cash into a buy only if it doesn't risk an unpaid rent before the game ends.
